title: Interest Is Owed on a Security Deposit
bodyText:
The city requires interest on a residential security deposit (B.R.C. 1981 sections 12-2-5 to 12-2-7). It is simple interest on the full deposit. The city manager sets the rate each December from one-year certificates of deposit and publishes it, and it applies to deposits provided in the next calendar year. For a tenancy of more than one year, figure the interest separately for each year, using the city's list of prior rates and its formula. Under a lease entered into before March 19, 2004, the rate is 5.5 percent a year.

The deposit stays the tenant's property. After the tenancy you may keep it or its interest only for actual cause under state law. The city's rule creates a duty to account for the interest, not a fiduciary relationship.

Before the tenant moves in, the written lease, rental agreement, site rules or other document you sign and give must say that interest must be paid on the deposit (section 12-2-4(a)(1)(F)).

Return the accrued interest within one month after the lease ends or the home is surrendered and accepted, whichever is later, following state law on returning the deposit and on notice and legality of deductions. Any interest that builds up after that is due when you return the deposit. State law lets a lease allow up to 60 days for the deposit, but the city section doesn't say that extends the month, so pay interest within the month.

If you keep any interest without giving the notice state law requires for keeping a deposit, you lose the right to keep any of the interest. Willfully and wrongfully keeping interest makes you liable to the tenant for $100 or three times the amount kept, whichever is more, plus reasonable attorney's fees and court costs, if the tenant gave at least seven days' notice before filing. In a tenant's suit under the city's rules you must prove that keeping the interest wasn't a violation, and the tenant can bring state and city claims in the same lawsuit. Wrongfully keeping the deposit itself has its own state penalties. A lease term waiving these rules is void (section 12-2-8).

Exception: the ownership and return rules (sections 12-2-5 and 12-2-6) don't apply to a deposit paid to a mobile home park for the lease of a mobile home space.
notes: B.R.C. 12-2-2, -4(a)(1)(F), -5 to -8 read; C.R.S. 38-12-103(1)(a). Not decided: whether the general penalty 5-2-4 also applies to 12-2-6(a). City page's 2026 rate and its lease-signing-date reading not adopted: the code ties the rate to the year the deposit is provided. REPLACES the state row's 'no interest is owed'; the state row's pricing-rule interest point isn't repeated. title: A Written Lease and Copies to Each Tenant
bodyText:
If you rent residential property for 30 days or more, enter into a written lease within 30 days after the rental begins (B.R.C. 1981 section 12-2-3). Don't rely on the 30 days: before anyone occupies the rental, you must also have signed and given the tenant a written lease, rental agreement, site rules or other document with the city's required disclosures, and have an accurate list of the people authorized to live there (section 12-2-4).

Give each tenant a copy of the lease within seven working days after it is fully signed, or within fifteen working days after any tenant signs, whichever comes first. State law separately requires a signed copy by the seventh day after the tenant signs (C.R.S. 38-12-801), so meet whichever deadline comes first.

Before a summons and complaint under section 12-2-3, the complaining witness or a city peace officer must first request a copy of the lease, and you have five working days from the mailing or delivery of that request to provide it. A lease term waiving these rules is void (section 12-2-8).
notes: B.R.C. 12-2-3, -4, -8 and C.R.S. 38-12-801(1) read. 'Any person renting' read as the landlord from its context. 'Working day' not defined in what was searched. The written-lease half overlaps statute-of-frauds-lease-term: split when the topic is settled. Round 1 independent check 2026-11-25; redrafted after reading the sections; round 2 not run.

title: No Renting a Building Heated Only by a Solid Fuel Stove
bodyText:
You may not rent out a building if a solid fuel burning device is its sole source of heat (B.R.C. 1981 section 6-9-6). The code's definition of sole source of heat speaks of woodstoves that are the only heating, so treat fireplaces, pellet stoves and other solid fuel devices the same way. A building doesn't count if it has a permanently installed furnace or heating system that uses oil, natural gas, electricity or propane, even one disconnected from its energy source (section 6-9-2). That exception answers only this city rule: state law still requires working heat (C.R.S. 38-12-505).

Any penalty falls on the owner, not the tenant. The fine is up to $100 for a first conviction, $200 for a second and $300 for a third, looking back two years (section 6-9-7).

title: A Working Toilet and Sewage System Is the Owner's Duty
bodyText:
The county's septic system regulations, which cover the whole county including its cities, make the owner of any structure where people live responsible for an adequate, convenient, sanitary toilet and sewage system in good working order (Weld County Code sections 30-1-20 and 30-4-10). Whether that also reaches a home on public sewer isn't clear, because the regulations say they apply to on-site systems (section 30-2-10), so treat it as applying. The regulations cover systems of up to 2,000 gallons a day; larger ones need state approval.

Sewage or effluent may not be discharged onto the ground or into state waters unless it meets the regulations' minimum requirements or state water quality standards, whichever apply. No one may build or maintain a dwelling without adequate sewage disposal; a failed septic system, or a condition the local health agency determines is a public health or safety concern, doesn't count as adequate. Cesspools, pit privies, slit trenches and seepage pits are prohibited. Don't connect more than one dwelling or other unit to the same septic system unless the application and permit specified it (section 30-4-140).

The owner or occupant must let the county in at reasonable times, on reasonable notice, to inspect, test, sample and monitor a septic system; if refused, the county may ask the District Court for an order (section 30-4-60). The county sends violation notices to the owner, and after a hearing on at least 48 hours' notice may order the system fixed within 30 days or its use stopped. The board of health may assess up to $50 for each day of violation (sections 30-4-160 and 30-4-170).
notes: W.C.C. 30-1-20, 30-2-10, 30-3-10 (Owner, OWTS, Failure), 30-4-10, -60, -140, -160, -170 read. Effective 2026-06-30 'upon adoption' per 30-1-30; adoption date not seen. City sewer rules not checked. Round 1 independent check 2026-11-25; redrafted after reading the sections; round 2 not run.

title: Septic Maintenance Is the Owner's Unless a Contract Assigns It
bodyText:
The county makes the owner responsible for maintaining a septic system unless a contract assigns that to a tenant, another party or a public body (Weld County Code section 30-13-10). This applies in the cities too (section 30-1-20). An assignment doesn't move the owner's duty to have a working system (section 30-4-10).

State law is stricter. Where the work is needed to keep a home habitable, you can move it to the tenant only for a single-family residence for which you get no government subsidy, in good faith, in a signed writing separate from the lease, with adequate consideration, if the tenant has the skills to do it, and never where it would endanger the tenant's health or safety (C.R.S. 38-12-506). A clause in the lease isn't enough.
notes: W.C.C. 30-13-10, 30-4-10, 30-1-20 and C.R.S. 38-12-506 read whole. State exclusions in 38-12-511 not read by me; case law not checked. Round 1 independent check 2026-11-25; redrafted after reading the sections; round 2 not run.
